name: STM32U031C8T6
title: STM32U031x4/6/8 ultra-low-power Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 56 MHz, 16 to 64 Kbytes flash, 12 Kbytes SRAM, 1.71 V to 3.6 V
summary: A Cortex-M0+ microcontroller family built for low power, clocked at up to 56 MHz from a 1.71 V to 3.6 V supply through an internal LDO, with 16, 32 or 64 Kbytes of ECC flash and 12 Kbytes of parity-checked SRAM (4 Kbytes of it kept through Standby). It has a 12-bit ADC with 16 external inputs and oversampling to 16 bits, a 12-bit DAC with sample-and-hold, one comparator, one op-amp with a PGA, a touch controller, a true random generator, four USARTs, two LPUARTs, three I2Cs, two SPIs, nine timers and a calendar RTC with tamper pins on a VBAT domain. Current falls to 52 µA/MHz running, 630 nA in Stop 2 with the RTC and 16 nA in Shutdown. Packages run from TSSOP20 and WLCSP27 to LQFP64 and UFBGA64; STM32U031C8T6 is the 64 Kbyte LQFP48 part with 39 I/Os for -40 °C to 85 °C ambient.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ with MPU, up to 56 MHz, 1 Kbyte instruction cache (ART)
16, 32 or 64 Kbytes flash with ECC; 12 Kbytes SRAM with parity (8 KB SRAM1 + 4 KB SRAM2)
VDD 1.71 V to 3.6 V; VDDA 1.62 V (ADC/COMP) or 1.8 V (DAC/OPAMP) to 3.6 V; VBAT 1.55 V to 3.6 V
Stop 2 630 nA with RTC / 515 nA without; Standby 160 nA with RTC / 30 nA without; Shutdown 16 nA; VBAT 130 nA with RTC
12-bit, 0.4 µs conversion, 16 external + 3 internal channels, 16-bit by oversampling
one 12-bit DAC channel, one rail-to-rail comparator, one op-amp with PGA gain up to 16
HSE 4 to 48 MHz, LSE 32.768 kHz, HSI16 ±1 %, MSI 100 kHz to 48 MHz (LSE-trimmed to ±0.25 %), LSI 32 kHz, PLL to 56 MHz
-40 °C to 85 °C (105 °C junction) or -40 °C to 125 °C (130 °C junction) ambient by order code

notes: (1) The flash memory can be put in power-down mode; it is not in power-down mode by default.

(3) SRAM2 keeps its content when the RRS bit of PWR_CR3 is set.
(4) A peripheral able to wake the device from Stop can ask for HSI16; HSI16 then starts and clocks only that peripheral, and turns off again once no peripheral needs it.
(5) UART and LPUART reception works in Stop mode and raises a wake-up interrupt on a start bit, an address match or a received frame.
(6) I2C address recognition works in Stop mode and raises a wake-up interrupt on an address match.
(7) Voltage scaling Range 1 only.
(8) In Standby each I/O can be set floating or given an internal pull-up or pull-down.
(9) The I/Os that can wake the device from Standby or Shutdown are PA0, PA1, PA2, PB15, PC5 and PC13.
(10) In Shutdown each I/O can be set floating or given an internal pull-up or pull-down; the setting is lost on leaving Shutdown.

circuits.title: Power supply scheme
circuits.description: VDD (1.71 V to 3.6 V) feeds the I/O ring, the regulator and the system analog circuits; every VDD/VSS pair gets a 100 nF ceramic and the device one 4.7 µF ceramic. VDDA/VREF+ feeds the ADC, DAC, op-amp and comparator and doubles as their reference, decoupled to VSSA/VREF- with 10 nF plus 1 µF. VBAT (1.55 V to 3.6 V) keeps the LSE, RTC and backup registers alive through the internal power switch when VDD is gone. The capacitors sit at or under their pins.
notes: One VDD pin and one VSS pin stand for all of them; each VDD/VSS pair has its own 100 nF.
Where a package has no VBAT pin, VBAT is bonded to VDD inside.
When nothing on VDDA is used, VDDA is best tied to VDD.

circuits.title: 8 MHz crystal on the HSE oscillator
circuits.description: An 8 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator between OSC_IN and OSC_OUT, a load capacitor from each end to ground, and a series resistor REXT between the crystal and OSC_OUT whose value is set by the crystal. The 200 kΩ feedback resistor is inside. CL1 and CL2 are normally the same, high-frequency ceramics of 5 pF to 20 pF matched to the crystal; the crystal's load figure is their series value, with about 10 pF allowed for pin and board capacitance.
notes: A resonator with built-in capacitors replaces Y1, C1 and C2.
The resonator and capacitors go as close to the oscillator pins as possible.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal on the LSE oscillator
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between OSC32_IN and OSC32_OUT with a load capacitor from each pin to ground clocks the RTC; the amplifier drive is chosen with LSEDRV. Stray capacitance CS, the pins' parasitic capacitance plus the board's, adds to CL1 and CL2. No resistor goes across the crystal: it is not needed and must not be fitted.

The crystal and capacitors go as close to the oscillator pins as possible.

circuits.title: NRST pin protection

The pull-up RPU and the input filter are inside. At every power-on NRST has to be able to rise above VIH(NRST) min or the device stays in reset, whatever NRST_MODE[1:0] in FLASH_OPTR selects, GPIO mode included.

operation.text: The Cortex-M0+ runs a two-stage pipeline with a single-cycle multiplier and an MPU, up to 56 MHz. A prefetch queue and branch cache (the ART Accelerator, 1 Kbyte) let code run from the 64-bit-wide flash as if it had no wait states at full speed. Flash is up to 64 Kbytes in one bank with ECC that corrects one bit and flags two, and records the failing address. SRAM1 (8 Kbytes, at 0x2000 0000) and SRAM2 (4 Kbytes, at 0x1000 0000 and also at 0x2000 8000 so the two run on) both carry parity and work at CPU speed with no wait states; SRAM2 can be kept in Standby and write-protected in 1-Kbyte steps.

Readout protection has three levels. Level 0 leaves memory open. Level 1 blocks flash reads and writes whenever the debugger is attached or the part boots from RAM or the bootloader; going back to Level 0 is possible with a 128-bit password and erases the backup registers. Level 2 turns off debug, RAM boot and bootloader for good. Write protection covers two areas per bank in 2-Kbyte steps. A hidden-protection (securable) area, set through FLASH_HDPCR and FLASH_SECR, becomes unreachable once its code has run until the next reset, which suits secure boot code.

The boot pin (shared with PF3 as BOOT0) and the boot selector option bit pick boot from user flash, system memory or SRAM. The system-memory bootloader reprograms flash over USART (PA9/PA10, PC10/PC11 or PA2/PA3), I2C (PB6/PB7 or PB10/PB11) or SPI (PA4 to PA7 or PB12 to PB15).

VDD (1.71 V to 3.6 V) feeds the I/Os, the regulator and reset, power management and internal clocks. VDDA, independent of VDD, feeds the ADC and comparator from 1.62 V and the DAC and op-amp from 1.8 V, up to 3.6 V, and is also VREF+. VBAT (1.55 V to 3.6 V) runs the RTC, LSE and backup registers through a switch when VDD is absent; packages without the pin bond it to VDD. VCORE comes from the internal regulator. If the VDDA functions are unused, VDDA is best shorted to VDD; a supply tied to ground takes away 5 V tolerance from the I/Os it powers.

Each supply pair is decoupled with ceramic capacitors as close to the pins as possible, or under them on the back of the board: 100 nF on every VDD/VSS pair plus one 4.7 µF, and 10 nF plus 1 µF on VDDA/VSSA. The 100 nF parts are good-quality ceramics.

POR/PDR holds the device in reset below its threshold in every mode except Shutdown, with no external reset part needed. The brownout reset can be set through option bytes to one of four rising and four falling levels. The programmable voltage detector compares VDD with a software-chosen level and can interrupt on falling, rising or both edges. Peripheral voltage monitors watch VDDA.

The main regulator serves Run, Sleep and Stop 0. The low-power regulator takes over in the two low-power run/sleep modes and in Stop 1 and 2, and in Standby it can keep SRAM2 alive. In Standby and Shutdown both regulators are off with their outputs high-impedance.

An internal supervisor switches the RTC domain between VDD and VBAT, taking VDD whenever both are valid. While VDD is within range a charger can trickle-charge a battery on VBAT through 5 kΩ or 1.5 kΩ (VBRS). External interrupts and RTC events cannot end VBAT mode, because VDD is out of range then.

Run is the state after reset. Sleep stops only the CPU. Low-power run uses the low-power regulator with the CPU at 2 MHz or less, from flash or SRAM; Low-power sleep stops the CPU from there. Stop 0, 1 and 2 halt all VCORE clocks and the PLL, MSI, HSI16 and HSE, keep SRAM and registers, and let LSE and LSI run; Stop 0 keeps the main regulator for the quickest wake-up, Stop 1 keeps the most wake-up sources, Stop 2 draws least. On leaving Stop the clock is MSI (up to 48 MHz) or HSI16. Standby switches VCORE off and keeps only the RTC domain, standby circuitry and optionally SRAM2; per-pin pulls can be held; NRST, IWDG, a WKUP pin, an RTC event or an LSE failure wakes it. Shutdown also stops LSI and has no brownout or VBAT switch-over; NRST, WKUP or an RTC event wakes it and the part restarts on MSI at 4 MHz.
While reset is asserted and as it ends, the I/O Schmitt triggers are off to save current. When the reset comes from inside, the NRST pull-up is switched off.

SYSCLK comes from the 4 MHz to 48 MHz HSE (crystal, resonator or external clock in bypass), the 16 MHz HSI16, the MSI (twelve steps from 100 kHz to 48 MHz, which the LSE can trim automatically to better than ±0.25 %) or the PLL, fed by any of those three and running SYSCLK up to 56 MHz. The 32.768 kHz LSE (four drive levels, or bypass) and the 32 kHz LSI (±5 %) clock the RTC; LSI also clocks the IWDG. RNG, USARTs, I2Cs, LPTIMs and the ADC can have their own kernel clocks. The clock security system moves SYSCLK to HSI16 if the HSE fails and can flag an LSE failure. MCO puts an internal clock on a pin and LSCO outputs LSI or LSE in the low-power modes except VBAT. AHB and APB run at 56 MHz at most.

CL1 and CL2 are high-quality high-frequency ceramics of 5 pF to 20 pF, normally equal. The load capacitance a crystal maker states is CL1 and CL2 in series plus pin and board capacitance, roughly 10 pF. The resonator and its capacitors go right at the oscillator pins to limit distortion and start-up time. AN2867 covers crystal choice.

Each GPIO can be a push-pull or open-drain output, an input (floating, pulled up or pulled down), an analog pin or an alternate function, and its configuration can be locked. GPIOs sink or source ±8 mA, or ±20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH; PC13 to PC15 source only 3 mA. The sum of all I/O currents plus the chip's own consumption stays within ΣIVDD and ΣIVSS.

An input with a pull resistor draws current when held at the opposite level, and an input at an in-between level draws Schmitt-trigger current. A floating input can drift to such a level or toggle with noise, so unused pins are set to analog mode or given a fixed level by a pull resistor or by making them outputs. ADC inputs are set to analog.

Seven DMA channels move data between peripherals and memories with four software priority levels, circular buffers and up to 2^16 - 1 items; DMAMUX routes any request line to any channel and can generate requests from trigger events. The NVIC handles 32 maskable lines, the NMI and ten core exceptions with four priority levels and tail-chaining. The EXTI detects edges on GPIOs and some peripheral signals, catches pulses shorter than its clock, and records wake-up sources even in Stop.

The 12-bit ADC has up to 16 external and three internal inputs (temperature sensor, VREFINT, VBAT/3), runs single or scan conversions, reaches about 2 MSps independently of the CPU clock, and switches itself off between conversions. Oversampling of up to 256 samples gives 16 bits. An analog watchdog flags conversions outside set limits; timers can trigger conversions; DMA can serve it. A calibration after every power-up is advised. Below VDDA = 2.4 V the analog switch booster (BOOSTEN in SYSCFG_CFGR1) is turned on, and off at or above it.

The sensor output rises linearly with temperature and is read by the ADC; its offset varies between parts, so uncalibrated it gives only relative readings. Each part carries factory readings at 30 °C (TS_CAL1) and 130 °C (TS_CAL2) taken at VDDA = 3.0 V, and the VREFINT reading at 30 °C, in read-only engineering bytes. VREFINT is the bandgap reference for the ADC and comparator.

One 12-bit channel, resistor-string with an output buffer that can be bypassed, 8- or 12-bit data, left or right aligned, with noise and triangle generation, timer or external triggers, DMA, buffer offset trimming, and a low-power sample-and-hold mode using an internal or external capacitor.

The rail-to-rail comparator has programmable hysteresis, speed and polarity; its reference is an I/O, the DAC, or VREFINT or 1/4, 1/2, 3/4 of it. It can wake the part from Stop and drive timer breaks and triggers. The op-amp has rail-to-rail inputs, low offset and bias current, a low-power mode, internal follower routing and a PGA with gains up to 16.

The touch controller measures surface charge transfer to sense a finger through glass or plastic, for keys, sliders and wheels, with up to 18 channels, three measured at a time on one sampling capacitor, spread spectrum, a max-count limit and end-of-acquisition flags. Channel count depends on package and free I/Os.

TIM1 is a 16-bit motor-control timer with four channels, three complementary outputs with dead time and a break input. TIM2 (32-bit) and TIM3 (16-bit) have four channels and encoder support; TIM15 and TIM16 are 16-bit upcounters with two and one channels, each with one complementary output. TIM6 and TIM7 are basic timers, mainly for DAC triggering. LPTIM1 and LPTIM2 run from LSE, LSI, HSI16, APB or an external input, keep counting in Stop and can wake the part. The IWDG (12-bit, LSI-clocked) runs in Stop and Standby; the WWDG (7-bit, system clock) has an early-warning interrupt. SysTick is a 24-bit down counter. All counters can freeze in debug.

The BCD calendar RTC has sub-second resolution, alarms, a 17-bit wake-up timer, 0.95 ppm digital calibration, reference-clock (50/60 Hz) correction, timestamp and five tamper pins, and nine 32-bit backup registers (20 bytes of user data kept by VBAT). It runs from LSE (also in VBAT mode), LSI (not in VBAT or Shutdown) or HSE/32. Its events can wake the device from any low-power mode.

Three I2Cs do Standard, Fast and Fast-mode Plus with 7- and 10-bit addressing and clock stretching; I2C1 and I2C3 have independent clocks and wake from Stop on address match. Four USARTs reach 8 Mbit/s with flow control, RS485 DE, SPI master/slave and half-duplex; USART1 and USART2 add smartcard, IrDA, LIN, auto baud and Stop wake-up. Two LPUARTs wake from Stop up to 220 kbaud and run 9600 baud from the LSE alone. Two SPIs run to 32 Mbit/s with 4- to 16-bit frames, NSS pulse, TI mode and CRC. Debug is two-wire SWD on PA13/PA14.

EMC results depend on the application and its software, so software-level EMC handling and prequalification tests are advised: plan for a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset and corrupted control data. Holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for one second reproduces most failures; ESD can then be applied within the rated range (AN1015).

Current into I/O pins from voltages below VSS or above VDDIOx is to be avoided. In characterization, injection into floating inputs counts as a failure when the ADC error exceeds 5 LSB TUE, neighbouring leakage leaves -5 µA/+0 µA, or the part resets or its oscillator shifts. Negative injection on an analog pin spoils conversions on others; a Schottky diode to ground on exposed analog pins is advised.

I2C timing meets the I2C-bus specification for Sm, Fm and Fm+ when the peripheral is set up correctly. Only FT_f pins meet the Fm+ low-level sink current. Every SDA and SCL I/O has an analog spike filter.
TJ must not exceed the maximum of the operating conditions. ΘJA is measured to JESD51-2 in still air; AN5036 covers thermal management.

Pin 1 or ball A1 and the marking areas are located per technical note TN1433. Parts marked ES or E, or shipped with an engineering-sample letter, are not qualified for production. On WLCSP27 the top shows product identification, date code (Y WW) and revision code, with the ball A2 identifier.
